title: Sales enablement prospect playbook: positioning, competitive briefs, pitch deck, pricing & security FAQ
author: Anika Patel
body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook gives SDRs, AEs, solutions engineers, and field marketing a single reference for Redwood Inference positioning, competitive talking points, an objection-handling library, a go-to pitch-deck outline, pricing guidance for common motions, concise case studies, and a security FAQ tailored to prospect conversations. Use this document as the canonical source for sales assets that require product/engineering sign-off.

Audience: Sales, Solutions Engineering, Customer Success, Field Marketing.

TL;DR Positioning and core message

- One-liner: Redwood Inference — production-first LLM inference that makes latency, cost, and reliability predictable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Primary value props (by buyer persona):
  - Engineering / ML Platform: "Unified runtime + tooling that removes the operational burden of serving LLMs at scale (batching, caching, routing)."
  - Product / App Teams: "Fast path from prototype to scale with consistent latency and cost controls — no model ops folklore."
  - Security / IT / Compliance: "Pin models, control network boundaries, and audit every inference via private deployments and enterprise controls."

Positioning pillars (short bullets to use in emails / decks)

1) Production economics: reduce cost-per-token while preserving SLOs via smart batching, KV caching and quantization profiles.
2) Unified deployment modes: same API and tooling across hosted, reserved (Dedicated), and Private/VPC or on-prem.
3) Reliability-first serving: SLA-backed Dedicated pools, automatic fallbacks, and predictable autoscale policies.
4) Developer experience: quick SDKs, clear performance profiles, and built-in evals to avoid regressions.

Competitive landscape (short brief)

Competitors to call out: Public cloud model endpoints (AWS/GCP/Azure managed endpoints), LLM API providers (single-model APIs), self-hosted inference runtimes (open-source frameworks + orchestration). Key differentiators to highlight in conversation:

- Compared to public cloud managed endpoints: Redwood focuses on high throughput + LLM-specific optimizations (KV cache, continuous batching) and provides consistent developer ergonomics across hosted/dedicated/private — public clouds trade flexibility for generality and often lack LLM-first batching/caching.
- Compared to single-vendor LLM API providers: Redwood offers deployment flexibility (dedicated capacity and private deployments) and transparent unit economics/recommendations for batching/quantization.
- Compared to self-hosted/open-source runtimes: Redwood provides a managed control plane, curated model catalog and SRE-grade SLAs; customers who run raw open-source stacks typically spend 6–12 months and ongoing headcount to match latency/reliability.

Competitive win themes and rebuttals

- Prospect: "We can host ourselves and avoid vendor lock-in."
  - Response: "Self-hosting increases time-to-value and operational risk. We reduce both by giving teams a clear upgrade path (self-hosted Private with Redwood control plane) and by providing performance and cost profiles that help you design for predictable production economics."
- Prospect: "The cloud vendor is already in our contract."
  - Response: "We partner with cloud providers — many customers use Redwood Dedicated in the same cloud account to get better LLM latency/cost without breaking compliance or cloud agreements."
- Prospect: "Pricing seems unclear for large-scale usage."
  - Response: "We provide straightforward usage and reserved capacity pricing plus example scenarios; we also run a short TCO assessment during POC to quantify savings from batching, caching and model selection."

Pitch deck — recommended slide outline (concise bullets per slide)

1) Title + 1-line positioning (what we do and who benefits).
2) The problem (latency variance, hidden token costs, operational load).
3) Market/Why now (open model ecosystem + need for predictable serving).
4) Redwood solution at a glance (hosted, Dedicated, Private).
5) How it works (serving runtime, kernel selection, smart routing, caching). Use a simple diagram (text description) — "client SDK -> control plane -> serving runtime (cache, batching) -> GPUs".
6) Developer and operator experience (API, Console, rollout patterns).
7) Performance/Cost examples (real numbers): e.g., "Customer A: 3x latency reduction, 40% token cost drop via batching & quantization."
8) Security & compliance (SOC2, audit logs, KMS integrations, VPC/private deployment).
9) Pricing & packaging (examples below).
10) Case studies (two brief stories).
11) Next steps / recommended POC (scope, duration, success criteria).

Pitch deck tips for SEs/AEs

- Timebox: aim for 20 minutes + 10 minutes Q&A.
- Tailor early slides (problem + impact) to the prospect's metric (latency, cost, compliance).
- Share a one-page TCO estimate during the POC planning call.

Pricing guidance (high-level — use as starting point for deals)

1) Hosted (self-serve): usage-based per-token pricing for generation and embeddings. Good for quick evaluation and low-to-medium throughput apps. Typical POC: 1–3 weeks, costs <$5k.
2) Dedicated (reserved capacity): monthly/annual committed SKU(s) for predictable throughput and SLOs. Ideal for mid-market / enterprise apps with steady traffic or strict isolation. Pricing levers: GPU class, reserved capacity units, burst capacity.
3) Private (VPC/on-prem): platform licensing + optional managed service/support. Contracted for customers with compliance or data residency needs.

Example pricing vignettes (illustrative only):
- SaaS startup (chatbot) — hosted: <$1k/mo initially; migrate to Dedicated when 1M+ tokens/day to reduce latency spikes.
- Marketplace with sensitive PII — Private deployment: license + 24/7 support; typical first-year ARR for Private customers: $250k+.

Discount & commercial guidance

- For Dedicated: standard discounts for annual commits + multi-year agreements.
- Include professional services days for model onboarding, prompt engineering, and eval setup in larger deals.
- Always validate expected token volumes and latency SLOs before proposing Dedicated sizing; coordinate with eng-serving-runtime for capacity estimates.

Sales play (step-by-step checklist)

1) Discovery: capture latency targets, monthly token volumes, model family preferences, compliance requirements, and integration constraints.
2) Technical qualification call: Solutions Engineer validates model compatibility and initial performance expectations.
3) POC scoping: define test prompts, success metrics (latency p95, cost per 1k tokens, accuracy/regression thresholds), timeline (2–4 weeks).
4) Run POC with production-like traffic; run A/B vs baseline where possible.
5) Deliver findings: performance report, suggested quantization/batching config, TCO.
6) Commercial proposal: present Hosted/Dedicated/Private options with pricing and onboarding plan.

Case studies (short, borrowable language)

1) Finlytics (financial analytics platform) — challenge: slow, inconsistent LLM latency harmed analyst workflows. Outcome: migrated to Redwood Dedicated; achieved 2.8x median latency improvement and reduced inference cost by 35% through batching + model selection. Quote: "Redwood gave us predictable latency during earnings week — the difference was night and day." — Head of Engineering, Finlytics.

2) Acme Retail (large retailer) — challenge: needing private inference for customer PII and seasonal scale. Outcome: Private deployment in VPC + managed support; zero infra incidents during peak seasonal traffic and improved cost predictability. Business impact: improved cart conversion for AI-driven recommendations by 6 points.

3) HelpHub (customer support SaaS) — challenge: escalating inference costs. Outcome: applied batching and prefix caching; achieved 40% lower per-conversation token costs and enabled 24/7 SLA with Dedicated pools.

Security FAQ for prospects (short Q/A for sales and SEs)

Q: Where does customer data live for hosted deployments?
A: Customer inference data is processed in region-specific clusters; we support data residency controls and can restrict processing to a chosen cloud region. For sensitive workloads we recommend Dedicated or Private deployments.

Q: How is data encrypted?
A: All data in transit is TLS 1.2+ encrypted. At rest, model artifacts and customer data are encrypted with provider KMS; for Private deployments customers can bring their own KMS/HSM.

Q: Do you provide audit logs and traceability for inferences?
A: Yes — Console and the control plane provide per-request traces, token-level cost breakdowns, and immutable audit logs for Dedicated and Private customers.

Q: What certifications and assessments do you have?
A: Redwood Inference maintains SOC 2 Type II. We regularly perform third-party penetration tests and provide summaries under NDA. For regulated customers we provide compliance evidence packages and can support additional assessments.

Q: Can you meet HIPAA/healthcare requirements?
A: We have customers in regulated industries; Private deployments with customer-managed networking and KMS are the recommended path for HIPAA workloads. Consult Security for scoping and a standard BAA workflow.

Q: How do you handle model privacy and updates?
A: Model versions are immutable once pinned for a deployment. We surface model change logs and provide controlled rollout patterns (canary, A/B, automatic rollback) so customers can validate new model versions against eval sets before full rollout.

Q: What controls exist to prevent data leakage into shared model caches?
A: We offer tenant-isolated caches for Dedicated/Private tiers. Hosted customers have per-customer logical isolation and we follow strict cache eviction and TTL policies.

Enabled artifacts (what to share after a meeting)

- One-page positioning (PDF)
- Slide deck template (editable PPTX / Google Slides)
- TCO worksheet (spreadsheet)
- Security datasheet (SOC2, pen-test summary)
- Case-study one-pagers (Finlytics, Acme Retail, HelpHub)

Appendix: SE talking points & config knobs to highlight

- Batching & autoscale knobs: discuss batch size targets, latency vs throughput trade-offs.
- Quantization profiles: explain cost/accuracy trade-offs and when to recommend 4-bit or 8-bit profiles.
- Smart routing: explain fallback policies (model variants, region fallback) and how they preserve availability.
- Eval and guardrails: mention built-in eval harness and regression alerts tied to prompt sets.
